claims.text: Cubic cobalt nanoparticles expose a higher fraction of under-coordinated edge and corner sites than spherical cobalt nanoparticles with random facet distributions.
The greater abundance of under-coordinated sites on cubic cobalt nanoparticles enhances catalytic activity.
The greater abundance of under-coordinated sites on cubic cobalt nanoparticles enhances catalytic selectivity.
The cubic cobalt nanoparticles predominantly expose {100} facets.
The spherical cobalt nanoparticles have a random distribution of facets.
Nanoparticle shape determines the relative abundance and distribution of under-coordinated edge and corner sites versus terrace sites.
The {100} facets preferentially exposed by cubic cobalt particles host a higher density of reactive, under-coordinated sites.
Under-coordinated cobalt sites enable stronger or more favorable adsorption of reactants and intermediates.
The proposed adsorption differences improve catalytic activity.
The proposed adsorption differences influence product selectivity.
Under identical reaction conditions, cubic cobalt nanoparticles will have a higher turnover frequency or other activity metric than spherical cobalt nanoparticles.
Under identical reaction conditions, cubic cobalt nanoparticles will have higher product selectivity than spherical cobalt nanoparticles.
The proposed shape effect is expected for cobalt-catalyzed CO oxidation or Fischer–Tropsch synthesis between 250 and 350 °C when composition and size are fixed and reconstruction is minimal.
Surface reconstruction or reshaping under reaction conditions could obscure initial shape-dependent differences in active-site exposure.
Electronic effects could influence catalytic performance independently of the proposed shape-dependent coordination effect.
A lack of a statistically significant activity or selectivity difference between shape-controlled samples would falsify the hypothesis.
Loss of the distinct particle morphologies during reaction would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary limits the hypothesis to conditions with minimal reconstruction, whereas the falsification rule treats loss of shape during reaction as falsification. Shape loss would instead place the experiment outside the stated applicability boundary and would not by itself refute the proposed effect when distinct shapes are maintained.

The mechanism states only that adsorption differences influence selectivity, without specifying a favorable direction, while the predicted outcome asserts that cubic particles will have enhanced selectivity.
